newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Battling Australia industry seeks budget sympathy.
newsitem.headline: Battling Australia industry seeks budget sympathy.

text.p: An Australian industry group on Thursday urged the government to spare manufacturing and engineering in the 1997/98 budget, saying the industries were struggling.
The Metal Trades Industry Association warned cuts to industry programmes in the current tough climate would fuel unemployment.
Manufacturing and engineering production was lower in the March quarter than at any time in the last 15 months, the association said in its latest quarterly survey.

"While expectations point to a recovery in the second half of the year, recent experience warns us not to be too confident that these expectations will come to fruition," association chief executive Bob Herbert said in a statement.
"On this basis, the upcoming budget should contain only good news to sectors doing it tough on any measure.
"Further cuts to industry programmes in this environment would be intolerable and, without doubt, lead to higher unemployment."
Treasurer Peter Costello is due to announce the budget for the fiscal year to June 30, 1998, on May 13.
The government is expected to slash spending by at least A$2 billion to balance the underlying budget -- excluding asset sales and state government debt repayments -- in 1998/99.
It has forecast an A$8.5 billion underlying deficit in 1997/98.
The association said 31 percent of the 250 companies surveyed for its March quarter poll were operating at very busy or busy levels, down from 40 percent in the December quarter.
This was 27 percentage points below the peak production activity level of 58 percent in the September quarter, 1994.
It also said the outlook for production remained subdued, with little improvement expected until the second half of the calendar year.
Capacity utilisation fell to 77 percent in the March quarter from 80 percent previously, and more than one-third of companies reported falling orders and sales in the March quarter.
Employment conditions also remained weak, with 33 percent of companies cutting staff. This rate of job cuts has been reported now for eight consecutive quarters.
The survey also found that business conditions remained highly competitive, with an increasing number of companies concerned about tough competition from imports.
It found 88 percent of companies were vulnerable to import competition -- the highest number for six-and-a-half years.
Export sales also trended down, with 25 percent of companies reporting lower exports and only 15 percent reporting increases.
